Section 01

Normal Phase vs Reversed Phase

01
CHEM 3400H

Normal-phase retention

Mobile phaseMostly nonpolar solvent
nonpolar moderately polar polar
Stationary phasePolar silica with surface Si–OH groups
injectionelution
Elutes firstNonpolar analytes stay mainly in the mobile phase.
Elutes lastPolar analytes interact with the silica surface.
Stronger solvent
Adding a polar modifier competes with the analyte for the silica surface, so retained compounds elute sooner.

Keep the mobile phase dry. Water changes the activity of bare silica and can shift retention.

CHEM 3400H

Reversed-phase retention

Mobile phaseWater with methanol or acetonitrile
polar moderately nonpolar nonpolar
Stationary phaseNonpolar bonded phase, commonly C₁₈
injectionelution
Elutes firstPolar analytes remain more comfortable in the mobile phase.
Elutes lastHydrophobic analytes spend more time in the C₁₈ layer.
Stronger solvent
Increasing the organic fraction usually decreases retention and moves peaks earlier.

Ionization, temperature, and the bonded-phase chemistry can change the exact elution order.

CHEM 3400H

Why reversed phase is widely used

Practical robustness

Aqueous–organic mobile phases accommodate many real-world samples and are straightforward to prepare, degas, and filter. Reversed-phase methods are generally reproducible, although full re-equilibration still requires several column volumes and depends on the column and starting composition.

Biological compatibility

Many pharmaceuticals, metabolites, and biomolecules are compatible with aqueous sample solvents, although cleanup, dilution, or solvent adjustment may still be needed to protect the column and avoid injection-solvent mismatch.

Reversed phase is the most common starting mode across pharmaceutical, environmental, and clinical HPLC because its selectivity can be tuned through organic composition, pH, and bonded-phase chemistry.

A nonpolar analyte moves between two environments

Retention builds through many small transfers between the mobile phase and the bonded phase.

Mobile phase
The analyte moves down the column while it remains in the flowing solvent.
More time in C₁₈ means a later peak
A more hydrophobic analyte usually spends a larger fraction of time in the bonded phase.

Section 02

Particle Size, Packing, and UHPLC

02
CHEM 3400H

Smaller particles preserve efficiency at higher velocity

Choose a particle and predict the operating trade-off.

Lower plate height means higher efficiency.
Particle design changes both the minimum H and how quickly H rises at higher linear velocity.
Pressure scales strongly with particle size. The graph compares efficiency, not pressure.
CHEM 3400H

Particle structure changes the diffusion distance

Fully porous

Pores extend through the particle. This gives high surface area and good sample loading.

Some molecules travel farther inside the pore network, which can increase mass-transfer broadening.

Superficially porous

A solid core sits inside a thin porous shell. The analyte only enters the shell.

The shorter diffusion path can provide high efficiency at lower pressure than a sub-2 µm fully porous particle.

Main trade-off Fully porous particles generally offer more loading capacity. Core-shell particles reduce mass-transfer distance.
CHEM 3400H

UHPLC supports the pressure and narrow peaks of small particles

Sub-2 µm particlesHigh efficiency remains available at faster flow.
Higher pressure hardwareMany UHPLC systems operate near 1000 bar or above, depending on the instrument.
Low-dispersion flow pathShort, narrow tubing and a small detector cell preserve narrow peaks.
Clean samplesFine particles and narrow channels make filtration and guard protection more important.
UHPLC performance depends on the full flow path
A UHPLC column on a high-dispersion system will not deliver its full efficiency.
CHEM 3400H

Column dimensions change speed, pressure, and solvent use

Choose the change you want to make.

Longer column
Plate number and pressure rise roughly with length. Resolution improves more slowly, approximately with the square root of length when other factors stay constant.

A 2.1 mm column needs much less volumetric flow than a 4.6 mm column at the same linear velocity.

A guard column takes the damage first

Sample
Guard
Analytical column
With a compatible guard
Analytes continue to the analytical column. Particles and strongly retained matrix collect in the replaceable guard.
Replace the inexpensive part
A rising pressure or worsening peak shape can signal that the guard cartridge needs attention.
CHEM 3400H

A short care routine prevents common column damage

1. Remove salts first
After a buffered method, rinse with a compatible aqueous mobile phase. Do this before introducing a high-organic solvent that could precipitate the salts.
Always check the column manualSilica columns often have a working range near pH 2 to 8, but modern stabilized phases may differ.
High pH can dissolve silica. Low pH can accelerate bonded-phase loss. Excess heat can shorten column life.

Key Takeaways

HPLC column selection

1

Match the phase polarity to the separation.
Normal phase retains polar compounds. Reversed phase usually retains hydrophobic compounds.

2

Particle size controls efficiency and pressure.
Core-shell particles shorten diffusion distance. Sub-2 µm particles require UHPLC hardware.

3

Column dimensions change the practical trade-off.
Length affects plate number and pressure. Internal diameter affects flow and solvent use.

4

Protect the stationary phase.
Use a compatible guard, control pH and temperature, remove salts, and store the column correctly.
